query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In a CoCrFeMnNi-based HEA multilayer system, increasing the lattice mismatch at the interfaces (thereby reducing interface coherency) will shift the dominant creep mechanism from diffusion‐mediated to dislocation‐mediated creep.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA multilayers (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with predominantly coherent interfaces
generation.intervention: Systematically modify the multilayer architecture to increase the interface lattice mismatch, creating semi‐coherent and eventually incoherent interfaces
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures relevant for creep testing (e.g., high-temperature nanoindentation or micropillar creep tests) with controlled stress conditions and in situ TEM characterization
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of interface coherency, as determined by the lattice mismatch between successive HEA layers
generation.mechanism: At coherent interfaces, enhanced atomic diffusion along the interface promotes diffusion-mediated creep. As the interface becomes semi-coherent or incoherent due to increased lattice mismatch, the diffusion pathways are disrupted and dislocation transmission is more strongly impeded, thus favoring dislocation-mediated creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: There will be a critical threshold of lattice mismatch beyond which the creep mechanism transitions from diffusion-controlled behavior (characterized by lower stress exponent and higher strain rate sensitivity) to dislocation-mediated creep (with higher yield strength and distinct dislocation motion observed via in situ TEM).
generation.baseline: Coherent-interface HEA multilayers exhibiting diffusion-mediated creep under high-temperature conditions
generation.boundary: At extremely high temperatures or very high applied stresses, mixed creep mechanisms may coexist; additionally, precise threshold values for the lattice mismatch may vary with alloy composition and processing parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The exact lattice mismatch value at which the transition occurs and the quantitative effect on the creep rate remain to be determined experimentally and via simulation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of CoCrFeMnNi-based HEA multilayers with systematically varied interface lattice mismatch by controlling layer thickness and compositional gradients. Conduct high-temperature creep tests using nanoindentation or micropillar setups while performing in situ TEM observations to capture dislocation behavior and interface evolution.
measurements: Creep strain rate vs. applied stress
Interface coherency assessment via high-resolution TEM and diffraction
Strain-rate sensitivity and activation energy analysis for creep mechanisms
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant change in the dominant creep mechanism is observed (i.e., if diffusion-mediated creep remains dominant even in multilayers with incoherent interfaces) or if the expected transition threshold in lattice mismatch is not identified, then the hypothesis that interface coherency controls the switch between diffusion- and dislocation-mediated creep in the HEA multilayer system would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. decision.trend: None of the provided references specifically investigate how interface coherency in high-entropy alloy multilayers governs the transition from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep. The earlier papers address HEA mechanical properties, phase stability, oxidation, and irradiation tolerance, but they do not resolve the open question of how tuned interface coherency might affect creep mechanisms in layered HEA coatings.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how precisely interface coherency in HEA multilayers shifts the dominant creep mechanism from diffusion-based flow (at lower stresses or higher temperatures) to dislocation-based creep (at higher stresses or lower temperatures). No referenced study has directly probed this microstructural lever—in particular, how adjusting interface mismatch or layer thickness influences the onset of the mechanism switch.
decision.lever: Fabricate a model HEA multilayer system with systematically varied interface lattice mismatch to span coherent, semi-coherent, and incoherent interfaces. Then perform targeted high-temperature nanoindentation or micropillar creep tests with concurrent in-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and complementary mesoscale dislocation modeling to correlate interface structures and the transition between diffusion and dislocation-driven creep regimes.
decision.why: Combining precise control of interface coherency in a layered HEA with in-situ advanced characterization and simulation will directly elucidate how mismatch affects creep pathways. This approach allows real-time observation of dislocations crossing interfaces under load and clarifies the interplay between interface diffusion and dislocation motion, addressing the outstanding gap in understanding creep mechanisms of HEA multilayers.
